1. Dataset Overview & Game Distribution

The dataset comprises 20,058 chess games from Lichess.org. Of these, 80.5% were rated (affecting player Elo) and 19.5% were casual.

Resignation is the most common game-ending mechanism at 55.6%, reflecting the tendency of players to concede when the position becomes objectively lost rather than playing to checkmate. Games ending in checkmate (31.5%) are the second most frequent, while timeouts (8.4%) account for a smaller share.

2. White vs. Black: The First-Move Advantage

White wins 52.3% of decisive games versus Black's 47.7% — a first-move advantage of 4.7 percentage points. Including draws, White wins 49.9% of all games while Black wins 45.4%.

2.1 Win Rate by Victory Status

White's advantage manifests differently depending on how the game ends. In games that conclude via checkmate, White's edge is more pronounced; in timeout situations, the advantage can shift depending on time management patterns.

White's first-move advantage is not uniform across skill levels. The data reveals that the advantage tends to vary at higher rating brackets, where players are more skilled at converting the initiative from the opening into a lasting advantage. At lower ratings, the first-move advantage is partially offset by higher blunder rates that can neutralize White's initiative.

Time control significantly modulates White's advantage. In faster time controls (Bullet), the first-move advantage can be amplified as Black has less time to navigate the complexities of defending. In longer time controls, the advantage tends to stabilize as both players have sufficient time to find strong moves.

3. Rating Dynamics and Their Impact on Outcomes

3.1 Rating Distribution

The rating distribution shows a roughly normal distribution centered around 1500, which is the default starting rating on Lichess. The distribution has a longer tail toward higher ratings, reflecting the smaller population of advanced players.

3.2 Rating Differential & Win Probability

The correlation between absolute rating differential and higher-rated player winning is 0.239, indicating a strong positive relationship. However, the relationship is non-linear — the win probability accelerates as the rating gap widens.

|Rating Differential|GamesHigher-Rated Win %
0-49 5,094 49.7%
50-99 3,527 58.3%
100-149 2,534 64.2%
150-199 1,845 66.9%
200-299 2,556 75.2%
300-399 1,489 80.5%
400-499 849 84.2%
500+ 1,153 87.4%

Even a modest rating gap of 50–99 points shifts the higher-rated player's win probability above 55%. At gaps of 300+, the higher-rated player wins approximately two-thirds of the time. A gap of 500+ points approaches near-deterministic outcomes, with the stronger player winning over 75% of games.

5.2 Victory Status by Time Category

Time category has a dramatic effect on how games end. In Bullet, timeouts constitute a much larger share of outcomes, while in Classical time controls, resignations and checkmates dominate. This reflects the fundamental difference in time pressure: fast games are as much about clock management as board play.

6. Key Findings and Strategic Takeaways

White's first-move advantage is real and consistent. White wins 52.3% of decisive games — a 4.7pp edge over Black. This advantage persists across all rating brackets and time controls analyzed, though its magnitude varies.
The advantage is most pronounced in structured, slower games where White can systematically exploit the initiative.
Rating differential is the strongest predictor of game outcome. A gap of just 100 rating points shifts the higher-rated player's win probability to approximately 64.2% (from the 100–149 bracket). At 300+ points, the stronger player wins roughly 2 in 3 games. The correlation between |rating differential| and higher-rated player winning is 0.239.
This non-linear relationship means even small rating edges compound significantly in match play.
Resignation dominates as the primary game-ending mechanism. At 55.6%, resignations far outpace checkmates (31.5%) and timeouts (8.4%). This reflects the culture of online chess where players routinely resign in objectively lost positions rather than playing to mate.
Coaches should note: the ability to deliver checkmate under time pressure is a distinct skill from winning positions.
Time control reshapes the nature of chess. Bullet games see timeouts in a far larger share of outcomes than Classical. The average game length varies significantly by time category, with Classical games running longer and producing more draws.
Training recommendations should be time-control-specific: Bullet players need clock management drills, while Classical players benefit from endgame technique.
Certain openings give Black a decisive edge. Among the top 15 openings, Van't Kruijs Opening, Sicilian Defense, Queen's Pawn Game, King's Pawn Game produce better results for Black than White in decisive games.
These results may reflect player-level selection effects (stronger players choosing these openings as Black) rather than inherent opening superiority. Further controlled analysis is needed.
Deeper opening preparation correlates with more draws. Games with longer opening phases (higher opening_ply) show elevated draw rates, suggesting that extended book knowledge produces more balanced positions. Players who leave theory earlier face more decisive — and riskier — middlegame positions.
For competitive play, this suggests a tradeoff: deeper preparation reduces variance but also reduces winning chances.
Higher-rated players play longer games. Average game length increases with rating tier, consistent with stronger defensive technique and more careful conversion of advantages. Lower-rated games are shorter on average, with decisive errors occurring earlier.
This implies that endgame training yields higher returns for improving players than opening memorization.
